clue.text: He pips boudoir machinations, but is manipulated by his wife

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the henpecked cleric who is so treated

indicators.note: machinations are schemings and contrivances, so these letters are worked into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A hen-pecked man outdoes the schemes of the bedroom yet is still ruled by his wife.
explanation.walkthrough: Trollope's henpecked Bishop of Barchester is bossed by Mrs Proudie; the definition describes him rather than naming him.
explanation.definitionFit: In Trollope's Barchester novels this cleric is famously dominated by his overbearing spouse.

clue.text: Eighteenth-century French politician, always cooking something up

definitions.meaning: a lawyer and deputy of revolutionary France
taken literally, a gastronome forever devising dishes

explanation.definitionFit: Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin sat in the Constituent Assembly and wrote The Physiology of Taste, the classic gastronomy book.

clue.text: Ironic interpretation, say, of old goat ()

indicators.note: say tells us the word is spoken, giving a sound-alike

parts.note: satire is ironic, mocking treatment of a subject

explanation.surface: A mocking reading of an elderly billy-goat.
explanation.walkthrough: The empty brackets are a printing artefact. 'Old goat' is a lecher, like the goat-legged woodland creature of myth.
explanation.definitionFit: A lecherous man is called an old goat, and the half-goat woodland deity of myth is a byword for lust.

clue.text: "James I remained an umpire whom no one consulted" (Hugh Trevor-Roper)

definitions.text: "James I remained an umpire whom no one consulted" (Hugh Trevor-Roper)

parts.words: "James I remained an umpire whom no one consulted" (Hugh Trevor-Roper)
parts.note: a quotation with one adjective missing before umpire; the solver supplies the historian's word for an all-knowing referee

explanation.surface: A historian's barbed verdict on King James I as an arbiter nobody asked.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation has a word dropped; Trevor-Roper's line reads 'an omniscient umpire', mocking the king's belief that he knew everything.
explanation.definitionFit: Knowing everything is the sense of the missing adjective, mocking a monarch's self-belief.

clue.text: Seventeenth-century French comic actor and playwright, always getting cooked up?

definitions.text: Seventeenth-century French comic actor and playwright
definitions.meaning: Raymond ..., comedian of the Hotel de Bourgogne
French for fish, a thing forever ending up in the pan

explanation.definitionFit: Raymond Poisson acted and wrote comedies in Louis XIV's Paris, and his surname is French for fish, food often cooked.

clue.text: Matricide, strangely so terse

indicators.note: strangely says the letters are set out in an odd new order

explanation.surface: A mother-killer, oddly tight-lipped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strangely' rearranges SO TERSE.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Agamemnon's son killed his mother Clytemnestra to avenge his father.

clue.text: Valley of the romantic novelist

definitions.meaning: Ethel M. ..., bestselling author of romances

explanation.definitionFit: A dell is a small wooded hollow, and Ethel M. Dell wrote hugely popular romantic novels.

clue.text: Iris Murdoch magician occasioning exodus

parts.note: points to a Murdoch title where a spell-casting figure is fled from

explanation.surface: A sorcerer in a Murdoch novel causes people to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: Murdoch's novel The Flight from the Enchanter: 'exodus' is the flight.
explanation.definitionFit: A sorcerer who casts spells, the figure fled from in Murdoch's 1956 novel title.

clue.text: Account by Marlowe and Hood of Turkish swimming trials?

definitions.meaning: a narrative poem written by Christopher Marlowe and later by Thomas Hood
the lover who swam the Hellespont nightly to his beloved's tower

explanation.definitionFit: Marlowe and Thomas Hood each wrote a poem on the Greek lovers; the youth swam the Hellespont, now in Turkey.

clue.text: Sort of care offered by Janet Frame

definitions.text: Sort of care offered by Janet Frame

parts.words: Sort of care offered by Janet Frame
parts.note: points to a Frame novel whose title names a hospital ward kind of care

explanation.surface: The New Zealand writer provides some kind of looking-after.
explanation.walkthrough: Janet Frame, a New Zealand novelist, wrote Intensive Care (1970).
explanation.definitionFit: Critical hospital care for the gravely ill gives the title of Frame's 1970 novel.

clue.text: Not much hair, say, for philosopher

indicators.note: say tells us the word is spoken, giving a sound-alike

parts.note: a lock is a small tuft of hair

explanation.surface: A thinker with thinning hair.
explanation.definitionFit: John Locke was the English empiricist who wrote An Essay Concerning Human Understanding.

clue.text: Men like Jim, Emsworth and Peter Wimsey in London arena

definitions.text: Men like Jim, Emsworth and Peter Wimsey
definitions.meaning: Conrad's Lord Jim, Wodehouse's Lord Emsworth and Sayers's Lord Peter are all peers

explanation.definitionFit: These fictional heroes are titled peers, and Lord's in St John's Wood is London's famous cricket ground.

clue.text: Farm-boy among Flora Poste's ethical problems

indicators.note: among says the letters lie within the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A young farmhand appears among the heroine's moral dilemmas.
explanation.walkthrough: Flora Poste is the heroine of Cold Comfort Farm, where Seth Starkadder is a farm boy; he sits in poSTE'S ETHical.
explanation.definitionFit: In Stella Gibbons's comic novel he is the brooding young Starkadder working the farm.

clue.text: Bad lot from Austria (gone now)

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A rogue who has left Austria for good.
explanation.walkthrough: The run is in austrIA GOne; 'now' merely completes the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Othello villain is the archetypal scoundrel, a bad lot.

clue.text: Practise Couéism?

parts.note: Coué's autosuggestion had patients repeat that every day they were getting better and better

explanation.surface: A question about adopting a self-help method.
explanation.walkthrough: Émile Coué's mantra, 'Every day, in every way, I'm getting better and better', describes recovery.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting better after illness is the verb, echoing Coué's daily mantra of improvement.

clue.text: Somehow not like a fantasist

indicators.note: somehow suggests the letters are got into shape in some way, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A dreamer described only as unlike something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somehow' rearranges NOT LIKE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oxford don wrote high fantasy, Middle-earth and The Lord of the Rings.

clue.text: Port for poetry as performance art

definitions.meaning: the 1960s ... poets made verse a live show

explanation.definitionFit: The Mersey seaport gave its name to the 1960s group of performance poets McGough, Patten and Henri.

clue.text: "If If drink oblivion of a day / So I the stature of my soul" (Meredith)

definitions.text: "If If drink oblivion of a day / So I the stature of my soul" (Meredith)

parts.words: "If If drink oblivion of a day / So I the stature of my soul" (Meredith)
parts.note: a Meredith couplet with a verb dropped before I in the second line; 'If If' is a misprint for 'If I'

explanation.surface: Meredith's lines on drinking to forget and so diminishing the soul.
explanation.walkthrough: Meredith's line runs 'So shorten I the stature of my soul'; the clue's 'If If' is a misprint.
explanation.definitionFit: To make smaller or reduce, the verb missing from Meredith's couplet about stunting the soul.

clue.text: Reflection of future royalty

parts.note: an author's upfront payment mirroring the earnings expected from sales

explanation.surface: A mirror image of a king-to-be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Royalty' looks like kings and queens; it is an author's royalty, and an upfront sum paid against it.
explanation.definitionFit: Publishers pay authors a sum ahead of publication, offset against royalties to come.

clue.text: Wandering Peter joins union to discover his muse

indicators.note: joins says the next piece is attached to the one before
wandering suggests the letters roam out of their usual order

explanation.surface: A roaming man enters a union and finds his inspiration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wandering' rearranges PETER to TERPE, which joins EU.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the Greek Muse of music and lyric poetry.

clue.text: Small collection reveals extensive rewrite

indicators.note: an extensive rewrite thoroughly recasts the word, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A slim anthology turns out to be heavily revised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extensive rewrite' rearranges REVEALS.
explanation.definitionFit: A handful, more than two but not many, a small number of things.

clue.text: Inverts, somehow, having struggled

indicators.note: somehow suggests the letters are got into shape in some way, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Someone turned things upside down after a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges INVERTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Past participle of a verb meaning to make great efforts, matching 'having struggled'.

clue.text: Michael Innes produced a grass one

definitions.text: Michael Innes produced a grass one

parts.words: Michael Innes produced a grass one
parts.note: Michael Innes was the pen name of J. I. M. Stewart, whose novel title names a plot of grass

explanation.surface: A crime writer is said to have made something out of grass.
explanation.walkthrough: J. I. M. Stewart, who wrote as Michael Innes, published An Acre of Grass (1965).
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of land area, the measured field of turf in Stewart's 1965 novel title.

clue.text: Quest of Dean Koontz

parts.note: points to Koontz's first novel, a science fiction book with Quest in its title

explanation.surface: The American thriller writer's search.
explanation.walkthrough: Dean Koontz's first novel was Star Quest (1968).
explanation.definitionFit: A heavenly body, the first word of Koontz's debut science fiction novel.

clue.text: Lady I mixed up with Miss Bennet

indicators.note: mixed up says the letters are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A noblewoman gets entangled with one of the Bennet sisters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed up' rearranges LADY I.
explanation.definitionFit: The youngest Bennet sister in Pride and Prejudice elopes with Wickham.

clue.text: American lawyer with stomach to produce a single fact

parts.note: DA is a District Attorney, a US prosecutor
tum is an informal word for stomach

explanation.surface: A US attorney with nerve establishes one fact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stomach' looks like nerve or courage; it is just the belly.
explanation.definitionFit: A single piece of information, the singular of data.

clue.text: Member of Norwegian peer group?

parts.note: peer here is the first name of Ibsen's hero, so the group is his family

explanation.surface: Someone belonging to a group of Scandinavian nobles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' looks like a nobleman; it is Ibsen's Peer, of the play Peer Gynt.
explanation.definitionFit: Surname of Ibsen's Norwegian hero Peer, so any of the family is a member.

clue.text: Merchant of films offers E. M. Forster adaptations

definitions.text: Merchant of films offers E. M. Forster adaptations

parts.words: Merchant of films offers E. M. Forster adaptations
parts.note: Ismail Merchant's film partnership made A Room with a View, Maurice and Howards End

explanation.surface: A film producer puts out versions of Forster novels.
explanation.walkthrough: James Ivory directed the Merchant Ivory adaptations of Forster's novels produced by Ismail Merchant.
explanation.definitionFit: The director James, partner of Ismail Merchant, whose name follows Merchant in the film company.

clue.text: Called upon again, like the seat of the Marchmains ()

definitions.text: like the seat of the Marchmains
definitions.meaning: Brideshead, the Marchmain family house in Waugh's novel title

explanation.definitionFit: To be visited a second time; Waugh's novel about the Marchmain family is Brideshead Revisited.

clue.text: They say man's offering this novel version of Goethe love-story

definitions.text: They say man's offering this novel version of Goethe love-story

parts.words: They say man's offering this novel version of Goethe love-story
parts.note: man's said aloud is Mann's, Thomas Mann's novel on the real woman behind Werther

explanation.surface: A man presents a fictional retelling of a Goethe romance.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Mann's 1939 novel imagines Charlotte Buff, model for Werther's heroine, visiting the aged Goethe.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Mann's novel about Charlotte Buff, the original of Goethe's heroine in Werther.
